{{Short description|Robust and nonparametric estimator of a population's location parameter}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Hodges–Lehmann estimator''' is a [[robust statistics|robust]] and [[nonparametric statistics|nonparametric]] [[estimation theory|estimator]] of a population's [[location parameter]]. For populations that are symmetric about one [[median]], such as the Gaussian or [[normal distribution]] or the [[Student t-distribution|Student ''t''-distribution]], the Hodges–Lehmann estimator is a [[consistent estimator|consistent]] and median-unbiased estimate of the population median. For non-symmetric populations, the Hodges–Lehmann estimator estimates the "[[pseudo–median]]", which is closely related to the population median.

The Hodges–Lehmann estimator was proposed originally for estimating the location parameter of  one-dimensional populations, but it has been used for many more purposes. It has been used to estimate the [[location parameter|differences]] between the members of two populations.  It has been generalized from univariate populations to [[multivariate statistics|multivariate populations]], which produce samples of [[vector space|vector]]s.

It is based on the [[Wilcoxon signed rank test|Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic]]. In statistical theory, it was an early example of a  [[R-estimator|rank-based estimator]], an important class of estimators both in  nonparametric statistics and in robust statistics. The Hodges–Lehmann estimator was proposed in 1963 independently by [[Pranab Kumar Sen]] and by [[Joseph Lawson Hodges, Jr.|Joseph Hodges]] and [[Erich Leo Lehmann|Erich Lehmann]], and so it is also called the "'''Hodges–Lehmann–Sen estimator'''".<ref>{{harvtxt|Lehmann|2006|pp=176 and 200–201}}</ref>

==Definition==
In the simplest case, the "Hodges–Lehmann" statistic estimates the location parameter for a univariate population.<ref>Dodge, Y. (2003) ''The Oxford Dictionary of Statistical Terms'', OUP. {{ISBN|0-19-850994-4}} Entry for "Hodges-Lehmann one-sample estimator"</ref><ref>Hodges & Lehmann (1963)</ref> Its computation can be described quickly. For a dataset with ''n'' measurements, the set of all possible two-element subsets of it <math>(z_i,z_j)</math> such that <math>i</math> ≤ <math>j</math> (i.e. specifically including self-pairs; many secondary sources incorrectly omit this detail), which set has  ''n''(''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)/2 elements. For each such subset, the mean is computed; finally, the median of these ''n''(''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)/2 averages is defined to be the Hodges–Lehmann estimator of location.

The two-sample Hodges–Lehmann statistic is an estimate of a location-shift type [[Difference (mathematics)|difference]] between two populations. For two sets of data with ''m'' and ''n'' observations, the set of two-element sets made of them is their Cartesian product, which contains ''m''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''n'' pairs of points (one from each set); each such pair defines one difference of values. The Hodges–Lehmann statistic is the [[median]] of the ''m''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''n'' differences.<ref name="Dic">Everitt (2002) Entry for "Hodges-Lehmann estimator"</ref>

==Estimating the population median of a symmetric population==

In the general case the Hodges-Lehmann statistic estimates the population's [[pseudomedian]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Hettmansperger|McKean|1998|pp=2–4}}</ref>  a [[location parameter]] that is closely related to the [[median]]. The difference between the median and pseudo-median is relatively small, and so this distinction is neglected in elementary discussions. Like the [[spatial median]],<ref name="Oja2010">{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|p=71}}</ref> the pseudo–median is well defined for all distributions of random variables having dimension two or greater; for one-dimensional distributions, there exists some pseudo–median, which need not be unique, however. Like the median, the pseudo–median is defined for even heavy–tailed distributions that lack any (finite) [[expected value|mean]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Hettmansperger|McKean|1998|pp=2–4 and&nbsp;355–356}}</ref>

For a population that is symmetric, the Hodges–Lehmann statistic also estimates the population's median. It is a robust statistic that has a [[breakdown point]] of 0.29, which means that the statistic remains bounded even if nearly 30 percent of the data have been contaminated. This robustness is an important advantage over the sample mean, which has a zero breakdown point, being proportional to any single observation and so liable to being misled by even one [[outlier]]. The [[sample median]] is even more robust, having a breakdown point of 0.50.<ref name="HW">Myles Hollander. Douglas A. Wolfe. ''Nonparametric statistical methods''. 2nd ed. John Wiley.</ref> The Hodges–Lehmann estimator is much better than the sample mean when estimating mixtures of normal distributions, also.<ref>Jureckova Sen. Robust Statistical Procedures.</ref>

For symmetric distributions, the Hodges–Lehmann statistic sometimes has greater [[Efficiency (statistics)|efficiency]]  at estimating the center of symmetry (population median) than does the sample median. For the normal distribution, the Hodges-Lehmann statistic is nearly as efficient as the sample mean.   For the [[Cauchy distribution]] (Student t-distribution with one degree of freedom), the Hodges-Lehmann is infinitely more efficient than the sample mean, which is not a consistent estimator of the median,<ref name="HW"/> but it is not more efficient than the median in that instance.

The one-sample Hodges–Lehmann statistic need not estimate any population&nbsp;mean, which  for many distributions does not exist. The two-sample Hodges–Lehmann estimator need not estimate the difference of two means or the difference of two (pseudo-)medians; rather, it estimates the median of the distribution of the difference between pairs of random–variables drawn respectively from the two populations.<ref name="Dic"/>

==In general statistics==

The Hodges–Lehmann ''univariate'' statistics have several generalizations in <!-- [[robust statistics|robust]] [[nonparametrics|nonparametric]] --> [[multivariate statistics|''multivariate'' statistics]]:<ref>{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|pp=2–3}}</ref>

*Multivariate ranks and signs<ref>{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|p=34}}</ref>
*Spatial sign tests and spatial medians<ref name="Oja2010" />
*Spatial signed-rank tests<ref>{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|pp=83–94}}</ref>
*Comparisons of tests and estimates<ref>{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|pp=98–102}}</ref>
*Several-sample location problems<ref>{{harvtxt|Oja|2010|pp=160, 162, and&nbsp;167–169}}</ref>
